subtopics.title: Two Sectors, One Set of Concepts

questions.question: The formal sector is defined by businesses that:
options: Are registered, keep full records, bank their money and answer to outside parties

questions.question: The central claim of this lesson is that the two sectors differ in:
options: The concepts they use to run a business
The recording of concepts, not the concepts themselves
Whether stock is held for resale

questions.question: Fixed assets are defined as:
options: Goods bought with the intention of reselling
Money the owner puts in to start the business
Possessions kept for use, not for sale
Amounts consumed in running the business

questions.question: The supermarket's R600 000 bank deposit and the spaza owner's R4 000 in cash are both:
options: Capital — the owner's resources committed to the business

questions.question: Chips bought for R8 and sold for R11 illustrate:
options: A loss of R3 per packet
Selling price minus cost price — a R3 margin, the same calculation in both sectors

questions.question: The spaza owner pays herself nothing. The accounting insight is that her labour cost is:
options: Zero, so her profit figure is perfectly accurate
Invisible — which quietly overstates her profit

subtopics.title: Where the Difference Bites — Records and Decisions

questions.question: A profitable spaza owner is refused a bank loan. The gain of formality at stake is:
options: Proof — unrecorded success is invisible success

questions.question: The cash tin doubling as the household purse violates:
options: The business entity rule — business and owner's money must be recorded apart

questions.question: The correct direction of the argument in this topic is:
options: Formal businesses need no business skill
Records replace the need for judgement
Recording adds proof, accuracy, separation and continuity to skill that already exists

questions.question: In a stokvel, the member list and payout roster correspond to the modern procedure of:
options: A ledger of contributions and claims

questions.question: Cattle as a historical store of wealth correspond most closely to:
options: Countable, visible assets — what an asset register records today
A liability owed to the community

questions.question: Grazing rotas with elders checking that nobody overgrazed implemented:
options: Internal control — agreed rules over resources, with trusted checkers

questions.question: Ma Dlamini's fridge and counter table are, in accounting vocabulary:
options: Fixed assets — kept and used, not sold

questions.question: The taxi fare to the wholesaler and the fridge's electricity are:
options: Expenses — money going out to keep the shop running

questions.question: Counting the tin at month end — what came in minus what went out — computes:
options: Profit — accounting's oldest equation, without a ledger

questions.question: The head said R1 800 profit; the notebook says R1 450. The R350 difference is:
options: A calculation error in the notebook
Small expenses that leaked from memory — taxi, electricity, airtime
Profit the notebook failed to count

questions.question: Multiplied over twelve months, the leak means the shop believes it made about:
options: R4 200 more than it really did
R350 more than it really did
R1 450 less than it really did

questions.question: Formal businesses write everything down because:
options: Nobody's memory can hold a hundred small expenses, and wrong numbers make wrong decisions

questions.question: In stokvel vocabulary, the December meeting where the treasurer accounts for every rand is:
The rule that a member cannot skip two months and still claim a payout is:
The takeaway of this topic is that Accounting:
options: Replaces indigenous practices with better ones
Formalises familiar community instincts — a sharper pen for existing wisdom
Was invented without any historical roots
